facts.statement: A four-year-old girl named Daisy Morris discovered the fossil remains of Vectidraco in November 2008 at Atherfield Point on the Isle of Wight.
facts.quote: In November 2008, Daisy Morris of Whitwell, Isle of Wight, a four-year-old avid natural history collector, discovered some small bones in a rock below the cliff face of Atherfield Point at the southwest coast of Wight.

facts.statement: The discovery was authenticated by paleontologist Martin Simpson in April 2009.
facts.quote: In April 2009, Daisy's discovery was authenticated by palaeontologist Martin Simpson, from the University of Southampton.

facts.statement: The species was formally described and named in a 2013 paper published in the journal PLoS ONE.
facts.quote: A scientific paper was published in 2013 about the find in the electronic journal PLoS ONE, titled A New Small-Bodied Azhdarchoid Pterosaur from the Lower Cretaceous of England and Its Implications for Pterosaur Anatomy, Diversity and Phylogeny.

facts.statement: Darren Naish, Martin Simpson, and Gareth Dyke described the type species Vectidraco daisymorrisae.
facts.quote: In it Darren Naish, Martin Simpson, and Gareth Dyke described and named the type species Vectidraco daisymorrisae.

facts.statement: The specific name daisymorrisae honors the discoverer Daisy Morris.
facts.quote: The specific name honours the discoverer Daisy Morris.

facts.statement: The only known specimen, a holotype from the early Aptian period 124 million years ago, was found in the Chale Clay Member of the Atherfield Clay Formation.
facts.quote: The only known specimen, holotype NHMUK PV R36621, was uncovered in the Chale Clay Member of the Atherfield Clay Formation of the Lower Greensand Group, a clay layer of the Deshayesites forbesi zone, Deshayesites fittoni subzone, dating from the early Aptian, with an age of 124 million years.

facts.statement: The preserved pelvis of Vectidraco is four centimeters long.
facts.quote: Vectidraco is a relatively small pterosaur. The pelvis is four centimetres long as preserved.

facts.statement: Based on its affinities, the authors assumed Vectidraco was toothless and likely had a crest on its snout.
facts.quote: In view of its affinities, the describing authors assumed it was a toothless form, featuring a crest on its snout.

facts.statement: A unique feature of Vectidraco is a triangular depression at the top rear corner of the hip joint, overhung by a ridge.
facts.quote: The hip joint is bordered at its top rear corner by a triangular depression. This depression is overhung by a ridge running downwards to the rear.

facts.statement: The rear blade of the ilium is uniquely T-shaped, ending in an upward-projecting expansion longer than the blade's shaft.
facts.quote: Furthermore, a unique combination of traits is present in that the elongated rear blade of the ilium is T-shaped, terminating in a wide expansion also projecting upwards, that is longer than the shaft of the rear blade itself.

facts.statement: The fossil shows camellate bone with internal air chambers, and all preserved vertebrae are pneumatized.
facts.quote: Damage to the ilium shows the presence of camellate bone, internal air chambers. Also all the preserved vertebrae are pneumatised.

facts.statement: Initially, Vectidraco was classified in a basal position within Azhdarchoidea, which would have made it one of the smallest members of that group.
facts.quote: Classification Vectidraco was assigned to the Azhdarchoidea, in a basal position. If correct, this would make it one of the smallest azhdarchoids known.

facts.statement: A 2018 study reclassified Vectidraco as a member of the family Tapejaridae, specifically as the sister taxon to Tapejara and Europejara.
facts.quote: In 2018, a study found Vectidraco in a more derived position within the Azhdarchoidea, more specifically as the sister taxon of both Tapejara and Europejara within the family Tapejaridae.

facts.statement: A 2020 phylogenetic analysis by David Martill and colleagues again placed Vectidraco within the family Tapejaridae.
facts.quote: In 2020, in a phylogenetic analysis conducted by David Martill and colleagues, Vectidraco was once again found within the Tapejaridae.

facts.statement: Vectidraco lived between 125.77 and 119.57 million years ago, spanning the Barremian to Aptian stages.
facts.quote: Time range: Barremian to Aptian (125.77 to 119.57 million years ago)
